problem.close: A password manager protects logins. Autofill wants a username and password, not forty lines of config.

holds.title: For what a login form cannot express

items.title: Configuration, verbatim
items.body: A whole .env file as one entry. No fields, no limits, no reformatting.

items.title: Keys that authenticate, not logins
items.body: API keys, service tokens, signing material. No username field, mostly.

items.title: The things you cannot re-issue
items.body: Recovery codes, 2FA seeds, a paper mnemonic. Findable, integrity checked.

items.title: Structured credentials
items.body: Real logins in proper fields, so a password manager can still autofill them.

compare.title: Why this is not another password manager
compare.lede: They solve a shrinking problem, better than this will. These are architectural differences.

rows.them: Their cloud. Self-hosting means running their server.
rows.us: One process on your machine. No third party exists.

rows.feature: What it is built to hold
rows.them: Structured login records with browser autofill.
rows.us: Free-form text and whole files, sized for configuration.

rows.them: You, and anyone who compromises the vendor.
rows.proton: You, Proton, and anyone who compels them.
rows.us: You. The key never leaves the server process and is never written down.

rows.them: Trust the vendor's audit, or read their source.
rows.proton: Open source, but trust the operator for your data.
rows.us: A SHA-256 seal per entry, hash-chained actions, re-checked live in the UI.

rows.feature: If you are forced to hand over the device
rows.them: Their product decides what the user can see.
rows.proton: Their product decides what the user can see.
rows.us: A panic key destroys the vault, and the wipe is audited.

rows.feature: From a shell, over SSH, in CI
rows.us: Yes. It is a CLI first.

rows.them: Free tier, then roughly $20 to $40 a year.

compare.footnote: Pricing changes. Check the vendors' pages. This table is about architecture.

notThis.title: What this is not
items: It does not autofill in your browser. Want that? Use 1Password or Bitwarden.
No sync, no phone app. Sovereignty over convenience.
No team or family sharing. No accounts, so nothing to share.
Aimed at people who run systems. Not for you? Use a password manager.
notThis.close: Logging in? Use a password manager. Deploy keys and .env files you cannot search? This is for that.

security.title: An architecture you can audit
security.subtitle: Four steps, all on your machine.
guarantees: No telemetry, no analytics, no outbound requests.
No account, no email address, no company holding a copy.
The master key lives in one process and is dropped when you lock.
A panic key wipes everything, and the wipe is audited.
MIT licensed, small enough to read end to end.
security.pipelineTitle: What happens when you save an entry

pipeline.title: Argon2id on your passphrase
pipeline.note: Memory-hard, 64 MiB, t=2, p=1, 16-byte salt. Never leaves your machine.

pipeline.title: A random master key
pipeline.note: One key per vault, generated on device. Your password only wraps it.

pipeline.title: AES-GCM 256-bit, fresh IV each time
pipeline.note: Own 12-byte IV per entry, so identical text never repeats.

pipeline.title: SHA-256 seal plus a hash chain
pipeline.note: Integrity seal per entry, chained actions. A silent edit breaks a link.

roadmap.title: The expansion is upward, not outward
roadmap.lede: A local vault is a niche only if that is all it is. Not if it is where rotation happens.

steps.title: Now: a local vault for long-lived secrets
steps.body: Today: .env files, API keys, recovery codes, config on your machine, with a checkable integrity chain.

steps.title: Next: leaked-secret detection and rotation
steps.body: Scan your repos against leak corpora. Show which keys still work, rotate them.

steps.title: Then: scoped credentials for AI agents
steps.body: Long-lived keys are how agent breaches happen. Scope one to a host, a window, an operation. Let it expire.

roadmap.close: None of it competes with autofill. All of it needs the key to stay on your machine.

items.a: No. It talks to a process on your machine over loopback. No network requests.

items.q: What happens if I forget my master password?
items.a: The 12-word recovery phrase. Lose both it and your password, and the data is gone.

items.q: Can I use it with no internet?
items.a: Yes. Offline once loaded. The CLI never touches the network.

items.q: Should I still use a password manager?
items.a: Yes, for your logins. Want autofill and family sharing? Use 1Password or Bitwarden.

items.q: Why is the key in a server process instead of the browser tab?
items.a: So extensions and XSS bugs cannot read your vault. The tab holds a token, not the key.
Yes. MIT, no paid tier, no entry limit.
